title: Best Exercise Bikes UK
short: Indoor exercise bikes compared by resistance realism, connectivity and comfort, from budget smart bikes to premium immersive trainers.
intro: An exercise bike's resistance system and screen quality matter more than raw price, since a bike that feels lifeless will get abandoned quickly. This guide compares bikes tested by Men's Fitness over at least a month each, pairing them with apps like Zwift and assessing build quality after sustained use.

products.name: Bike+ with Peloton IQ
products.best_for: Buyers who want the most immersive, motivating workout experience
products.key_spec: Swivelling HD touchscreen, front-facing camera for movement tracking, Sonos audio
products.summary: Men's Fitness found this one of the most immersive and motivating indoor fitness experiences money can buy, with Peloton IQ's built-in camera tracking movement during strength classes like a personal trainer watching your form. A vast, high-quality class library and swivel screen make it a full-body training hub, though the subscription is essential to unlock its full value.
pros: Peloton IQ adds off-bike workout tracking
cons: High upfront cost plus essential subscription
Power metrics may not satisfy data-driven cyclists
products.search: Peloton Bike Plus with Peloton IQ

products.name: Atom
products.best_for: Serious cyclists who want precise, data-rich training
products.key_spec: 22 integrated gears, crank position read 1,000 times/second, Smart resistance mode
products.summary: The number one exercise bike in public gyms and elite fitness spaces, Men's Fitness found it sturdy enough for years of abuse yet precise enough for exact shifting. The Wattbike Hub's pedal efficiency score and training plans let you replicate tough pro-circuit climbs, though it's noisy and geared more toward experienced cyclists.
pros: Wealth of insights via Wattbike Hub
cons: Feels geared more toward experienced cyclists

products.name: TACX Neo Bike Plus
products.best_for: Buyers who want the most authentic outdoor-riding feel indoors
products.key_spec: Built-in road-surface simulation motor, climbs up to 25%, programmable shifters
products.summary: Men's Fitness calls this the pinnacle of exercise bikes, with a built-in motor replicating the 'rumble' of cobbles or gravel and resistance mimicking climbs up to 25%. Programmable shifters mimic Shimano, SRAM or Campagnolo, and it pairs with Zwift, Strava and TrainerRoad for a genuinely immersive ride, though the drop bars have some flex.
pros: Immersive real-road feel with surface rumble
cons: Some flex in the drop bars

products.name: VeloCore
products.best_for: Buyers who want their bike to also work their core and arms
products.key_spec: Tilting lean mode, 100 resistance levels, includes 1-year JRNY app membership
products.summary: No bike works the core quite like the VeloCore, which morphs from a stationary bike to a tilting one at the press of a button, adding a whole new dimension to workouts. Men's Fitness found the ride smooth and quiet with a large screen in two sizes, though the design is bigger and heavier than most indoor bikes.
pros: Unique leaning feature targets core and arms
Free year of JRNY app included
cons: Bigger and heavier than most indoor bikes

products.name: AssaultBike Classic
products.best_for: Buyers who want a simple, brutal calorie-torching workout
products.key_spec: Air resistance flywheel, belt drive, upgradable/replaceable parts
products.summary: The original air bike still found in commercial gyms everywhere, with Men's Fitness praising its dialled-in ergonomics and super-smooth belt drive. Almost every part can be upgraded or replaced as an aftermarket purchase, making it a genuinely long-term investment, though the console can be hard to read.
cons: Console can be hard to read

products.name: Smart Bike
products.best_for: Buyers who want smart features without a four-figure price tag
products.summary: Refreshingly affordable against rivals costing two grand or more, Men's Fitness found it well made and easy to set up despite the lower price, with a stylish design that won't look out of place at home. There's no built-in screen, relying instead on the Apex app via your own device, and the seat can be slightly uncomfortable.
pros: Well made and easy to set up
Extensive class and instructor library via app

guide.q: Do I need a screen built into the bike?
guide.a: A built-in screen, like the Peloton or Bowflex here, gives the most seamless experience but adds significantly to the cost. A screen-free bike like the Apex, paired with your own phone or tablet, gives access to similar app-based classes at a much lower price if you don't mind propping up a device.

guide.q: What resistance type should I choose?
guide.a: Magnetic or electronic resistance, found on most smart bikes here, gives smooth, quiet, app-controlled adjustment. Air resistance, like the AssaultBike here, gets harder the faster you pedal, giving an intense, simple workout with no subscription needed. Realistic road-feel systems, like Garmin's TACX Neo, add simulated gradient and surface texture for outdoor-like immersion.

guide.q: Is a subscription worth the ongoing cost?
guide.a: A subscription unlocks the class libraries and structured training plans that make premium bikes like the Peloton or Wattbike genuinely motivating long-term. If you'd rather just pedal without guided content, a subscription-free option like the AssaultBike Classic avoids that recurring cost entirely.

guide.q: How much floor space does an exercise bike actually need?
guide.a: The bike's main body is often fairly compact, but check the footprint of the stabiliser stand and any handlebar extensions or screen housings, which can extend well beyond the bike itself. This overhang matters most if you're fitting a bike into a smaller room rather than a dedicated home gym.
